hints: Look for the word 'all' in each option. Ask yourself which virus structure is truly universal and which ones vary between different viruses.

Remember the basic virus plan: nucleic acid inside plus a protein coat outside. Think about whether that nucleic acid is always RNA, whether an envelope is always present, and whether viruses ever make their own proteins.
walkthrough:
**Recall the universal virus structure**

Think of a virus in the simplest way. It is just genetic material wrapped in a protective protein coat.

That protein coat is called the capsid, and every virus has one to protect its nucleic acid.

**Sort universal features from variable features**

The nucleic acid can be either DNA or RNA, not always RNA. Some viruses have DNA, like adenovirus, and some have RNA, like HIV.

Only some viruses have an outer lipid envelope taken from the host cell membrane. Many, like tobacco mosaic virus, are non-enveloped.

**Remember why viruses have no ribosomes**

Viruses do not carry out protein synthesis themselves. They have no ribosomes at all, neither 70S nor 80S.

They hijack the host cell 80S ribosomes to make new viral proteins. So A is the only statement true for all viruses.

options.A: Correct. All viruses have a protein capsid surrounding their nucleic acid for protection and attachment.
options.B: Not all viruses contain RNA. Some have DNA as their genetic material instead.
options.C: Only enveloped viruses have a phospholipid envelope. Many viruses are non-enveloped and have only the capsid.
options.D: Viruses contain no ribosomes at all. They use the host cell ribosomes to make viral proteins.
